recent_posts.title: Tesla files bespoke Roadster badge trademark as nine-year-old supercar promise nears a reveal that has been pushed back every year since 2020
recent_posts.summary: Tesla filed two trademark applications with the USPTO on April 28 for a bespoke Roadster badge — a triangular shield with a custom wordmark and a vehicle silhouette — marking the first standalone vehicle branding Tesla has created outside of the Cybertruck. The Roadster was originally unveiled as a prototype in November 2017 with a promised 2020 delivery, but has never entered production. Elon Musk stated during Tesla's Q1 2026 earnings call that a reveal is expected in late May or early June 2026, with production potentially starting 12–18 months after that. Meanwhile, the electric supercar market has matured significantly since 2017, with competitors like Rimac Nevera, Lucid Air Sapphire, and Pininfarina Battista now matching or exceeding the Roadster's original specs. The trademark filing signals Tesla's intent to position the Roadster as a true supercar brand rather than a technology product, but no physical car has been produced.

recent_posts.title: Meta takes Ofcom to court over Online Safety Act fee methodology
recent_posts.summary: Meta has filed a judicial review against UK regulator Ofcom, challenging the methodology used to calculate fees and penalties under the Online Safety Act. The core dispute is whether fines and levies should be based on global qualifying worldwide revenue or UK-only revenue. While the annual fees are modest for Meta, the penalty exposure is significant — up to 10% of worldwide revenue, potentially reaching $16bn. The first invoices are expected in September 2025, giving Meta urgency to resolve the methodology before billing begins. A ruling in Meta's favor would also affect TikTok, X, Snap, and other large platforms subject to the same framework. The case is procedural, not constitutional — Meta argues Ofcom's interpretation exceeds Parliament's intent and is disproportionate under public-law principles.

recent_posts.title: Google launches $100 screenless Fitbit Air with Gemini AI health coach at $10
recent_posts.summary: Google has launched the Fitbit Air, a $100 screenless fitness band weighing 12 grams that tracks heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and HRV. The device has no display or buttons and relies entirely on a companion app. The real product is a $10/month Google Health subscription powered by a Gemini AI coach that interprets sensor data, designs workout plans, and analyzes meal photos for nutrition. The launch coincides with a forced migration of all Fitbit user data to Google accounts by May 19, with data deletion starting July 15 for non-migrators. The Fitbit Air directly targets Whoop's screenless wearable model but undercuts its subscription cost by more than half. Google is positioning the Fitbit brand as platform-neutral, launching on both iOS and Android, prioritizing subscription revenue over ecosystem lock-in. Privacy concerns surround the migration of sensitive health data into Google's account infrastructure amid ongoing GDPR scrutiny in Europe.

recent_posts.title: NorthC data centre fire in Almere knocks Utrecht University offline and disables public transport emergency system across Utrecht province
recent_posts.summary: A fire at NorthC's data centre in Almere, Netherlands caused widespread disruption: Utrecht University went offline, public transport emergency communications across Utrecht province failed, and an NL-Alert was issued to Flevoland residents. The incident revealed that Transdev's regional transport control centre servers had no backup location, leaving bus and tram drivers without emergency communication. The fire escalated to GRIP 1 status within 40 minutes, and the emergency electricity installation was declared a total loss. The event echoes the 2021 OVHcloud Strasbourg fire and highlights a recurring structural problem: organisations hosting critical systems in single data centres without tested failover plans, regardless of the facility's Tier 3+ redundancy rating.

recent_posts.title: ShinyHunters breach Instructure Canvas LMS, claim 275M users and 3.65TB of student data from 9,000 schools including 44 Dutch institutions
recent_posts.summary: ShinyHunters, the criminal group behind the Snowflake supply chain attacks, has breached Instructure — the company behind Canvas LMS — claiming 3.65TB of data from 275 million users across 9,000 educational institutions worldwide. The stolen data includes names, email addresses, student IDs, and private messages between students and educators. Forty-four Dutch universities and schools are confirmed affected. This is Instructure's second breach in eight months by the same group. The incident highlights the structural risk of vendor concentration in edtech: schools had no control over the vendor's security posture yet bear the consequences. Instructure has been given a ransom deadline of 8 May or the data goes public. The breach also exposes a regulatory gap where GDPR and NIS2 compliance at the institutional level cannot prevent failures at the vendor level.

recent_posts.title: Silicon Valley spends $25M backing Matt Mahan for California governor but polls show 4% as Hilton and Steyer lead June primary
recent_posts.summary: Silicon Valley has poured over $25 million into San Jose mayor Matt Mahan's California gubernatorial campaign, with backers including Sergey Brin, Reed Hastings, and Steve Huffman. Despite the massive financial support, Mahan polls at just 4% with the June 2 primary weeks away, trailing Steve Hilton (20%), Tom Steyer (18%), and Xavier Becerra (10%). The campaign reflects a broader tech industry strategy to reshape California politics, including a proposed $500M endowment (California Renewal) to fund long-term political activity and opposition to a billionaire wealth tax ballot measure. The piece draws parallels to past tech-backed California campaigns that failed despite massive spending, and frames the effort as Silicon Valley building a political machine rather than simply backing one candidate.

recent_posts.title: How AI Orchestration Layers Are Reshaping the Car Buying Experience
recent_posts.summary: BadCo.AI is developing a CRM-native AI orchestration platform aimed at transforming the car buying experience. The platform connects dealership CRM systems, inventory feeds, financing tools, and dealer management systems into a unified decision engine. A key feature is the patent-pending Intelligent Desking™ platform, which lets buyers explore real-time payment configurations and financing scenarios in a single continuous interaction. The orchestration layer maintains persistent conversational context across voice, SMS, and chat channels, enabling buyers to progress without re-explaining their needs. The platform also addresses dealership operational challenges such as unanswered service calls and slow follow-ups, while supporting regulatory transparency requirements around pricing disclosures.

recent_posts.title: Tata and JSW to spend $1bn building India’s way out of Chinese battery dependence
recent_posts.summary: Tata Group and JSW Group are each funding separate R&D centres focused on next-generation battery chemistries and advanced EV systems, with a combined investment of nearly $1bn. The move is driven by India's heavy dependence on Chinese battery cells, materials, and equipment — a vulnerability that has become acute as Beijing tightens export controls on graphite, lithium-processing equipment, and battery-making machinery. Tata's effort is housed within Agratas, its battery arm already building a 20 GWh gigafactory in Gujarat, while JSW is operating through its JNEXT technology centre in Pune. Neither group expects to displace Chinese chemistry leadership this decade; the realistic goal is enough internal capability to specify, validate, and negotiate from a stronger position. The push mirrors Europe's battery sovereignty drive post-Northvolt, and complements India's existing PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells by finally adding private R&D capital to the equation.

recent_posts.title: Amazon retreats from Singapore groceries, leans on cross-border instead
recent_posts.summary: Amazon is shutting down Amazon Fresh and its local fulfilment operations in Singapore on 6 July 2026, ending grocery partnerships with Little Farms and AS Watson. A small number of roles will be cut. The decision reflects demand data showing Singaporean shoppers prefer cross-border purchases from US, Japanese, and German catalogues over locally stocked goods. AWS, retail, and Global Selling operations remain unaffected, with Amazon having committed S$12 billion to cloud infrastructure in Singapore. The closure fits a broader Amazon pattern of exiting grocery and retail ventures lacking scale or differentiation, including shutting US Amazon Go and Amazon Fresh stores and narrowing its grocery footprint to Whole Foods.

recent_posts.title: Quantum Motion lands $160m in EU’s first major late-stage commitment
recent_posts.summary: The EU's new Scaleup Europe Fund has made its first investment, leading a $160m round in UK-based Quantum Motion, a silicon-CMOS spin-qubit company. This is the largest single funding round for any European silicon-spin-qubit company and notably includes a post-Brexit UK company, clarifying the fund's eligibility scope. Quantum Motion's approach uses standard silicon-CMOS manufacturing — the same process used by the broader semiconductor industry — trading short-term performance for long-term scalability and manufacturability. Recent milestones include delivering a full-stack quantum computer to the UK's National Quantum Computing Centre and advancing to DARPA QBI Stage B. The round roughly doubles the company's total cumulative capital and signals EU strategic intent to compete with US deeptech funding at scale, with a utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing target in the 2030s.
